newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan victors say take foes' provincial capital.
newsitem.headline: Afghan victors say take foes' provincial capital.

text.p: Afghanistan's victorious Taleban Islamic militia said it had captured the Parwan province capital of Charikar north of Kabul on Saturday, driving out the forces of ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Taleban sources, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, said the militia was heading further north towards the ousted government's military base of Jabal-us-Seraj. There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report.
Taleban earlier said it believed Rabbani and his aides fled to Jabal-us-Seraj before the militia captured the national capital Kabul and set up its own government there on Friday.

Rabbani said in a statement on Friday his administration had shifted from Kabul to Parwan and the adjoining Kapisa province and was "carrying out, among other tasks, security and defence affairs" from there.
AIP quoted Taleban sources as saying at least 18 pro-Rabbani fighters were killed and several captured in the Charikar fighting, compared to only five Taleban men killed.

Taleban's self-declared government said it had hanged two more "accomplices" of executed former president Najibullah on Friday evening, naming them as his bodyguard, General Jafsar, and his aide Tokhi.
Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were themselves executed soon after the Taleban entered Kabul on Friday.
All four had been housed at a U.N. compound in Kabul since Najibullah was ousted in April 1992.
The fly-blown bodies of Najibullah and Shahpur were still hanging on Saturday from a concrete traffic post outside the presidential palace. There was no sign of the bodies of Jafsar and Tokhi.

The ousted government on Friday called on the world not to recognise the fundamentalist Islamic regime decreed by the Taleban militia, which moved quickly to bar women workers from offices and promised death for adulterers and drinkers.
The official Kabul Radio broadcast a message from Taleban's supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar that said his movement wanted good relations with all peace-loving countries.
In other developments, the United States expressed hope that the Taleban would move toward reconciliation and held out the possibility of establishing full diplomatic ties.
China voiced concern on Saturday about the fighting and said it hoped for peace and reconciliation. However, Beijing stopped short of recognising the Taleban administration.
In New Delhi, Amnesty International's Indian unit criticised the killing of Najibullah and called on governments to stop human rights abuses in Afganistan.

Kabul Radio urged those who had fled the capital fearing bloodshed to return and said government employees should report for work. But one employee who turned up at the Reconstruction Ministry with his colleagues found the doors locked.
A Taleban preacher at a mosque in the diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan district said all men should wear either the traditional skull caps or turbans to conform with strict Islamic tenets.
Religious scholar Mullah Agha Gulabi told the radio that adulterers and drinkers must be killed.
"God says that those committing adultery should be stoned to death," he said.

"Anybody who drinks and says that it is not against the Koran, you have to kill him and hang his body for three days until people say this is the body of the drinker who did not obey the Koran and Allah's order."
Taleban fighters patrolled Kabul in pick-up trucks on Saturday, but there was no sign of tension as Kabul resumed normal life after the Friday weekend.
Relief agencies said they hoped to begin flights from Kabul airport as soon as they get security clearances from Taleban.
Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai, the ousted government's deputy foreign minister who is attending the U.N. General Assembly session in New York, blamed Pakistan for the Taleban's success.
Pakistan appeared to signal the first recognition of the new regime on Friday by announcing it would send officials to Kabul.
The Taleban appear to control well over half the country, which has suffered continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops withdrew in 1989.

At the U.N., a draft statement prepared by Russia expressed grave concern about the "scale and the intensification of the military confrontation in Afghanistan, including the seizure of the capital city of Kabul by the Taleban."
